input: This inventory policy concerns a spare motor, and it sets out the basis on which safety stock is to be held for the item. Mean demand is 1400 units per week, with a standard deviation of 306 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 8 weeks, which is a considerable interval over which demand has to be covered before fresh stock can arrive. On the basis of these figures, the safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 1428 units, a substantial holding that reflects both the scale of weekly demand and the length of the replenishment cycle. It is important to note the assumptions on which the policy rests. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks, and seasonal peaks are excluded, which means that the policy is calibrated to the ordinary run of demand rather than to the exceptional demand that can arise at particular times of the year. In other words, the safety stock is designed to absorb the normal week-to-week fluctuation in demand over the lead time at the chosen service level, and it should not be expected to provide the same degree of protection during seasonal peaks, when demand is likely to be systematically higher than the average on which the calculation has been based. Overall, the policy provides a clearly defined stockholding rule for the spare motor under the stated conditions.
target:
Safety stock for the spare motor is 1428 units, set for a 95% cycle service level. Mean demand is 1400 units per week, the standard deviation of demand is 306 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 8 weeks. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks, and seasonal peaks are excluded from the policy.

Safety stock covers demand variability over the replenishment interval. Demand in a single week varies around its mean, and the lead time stretches that variability over the whole wait for replenishment, so the stock held above mean lead-time demand is what absorbs a run of heavy weeks without emptying the store. The service level fixes how much of that variability the stock is sized to absorb: the policy accepts stock-outs in the share of cycles that falls beyond the stated level, and that acceptance is part of the figure, not a defect in it.

The assumptions bound the result. Independence between weeks means a heavy week carries no information about the week that follows, and the normal treatment sets the shape of the demand spread that the stock is sized against. Seasonal peaks stand outside the policy: demand in a peak season is not drawn from the stated distribution, and stock sized on the stated mean and spread will run short in a peak season more often than the service level suggests. The policy therefore holds for ordinary demand over the stated lead time, and it is reopened when the lead time, the demand mean, or the demand spread changes materially.
